entry.title: Speculative decoding lands on Metal - Qwen 3.8's NextN head and Gemma 4's assistant drafter.
entry.content: Both drafter families that ship with their models now run on any Apple GPU dasLLAMA runs on, and the depth is a per-box knob the tuner mints. Measured against a stock llama.cpp on identical rendered prompts: gemma-4-26B-A4B on an M5 Max goes 122.7 to 145.9 tok/s at depth 1 (llama.cpp 97.7 to 133.7), Qwen3.8-27B on an M4 Pro 12.7 to 14.0 (llama.cpp 11.5 to 13.8). How we measured, what we tried, and why the gain is as small as it is: the story.

entry.title: The model that drafts its own next token.
entry.content:
We turned speculative decoding on, and Anton's Mac mini got slower. That was the morning of the 2nd of September, and it is why this story has a second day.

The idea first. A model generates one token at a time, and for a big model every token costs a full pass over the weights. Speculative decoding lets a small drafter propose a few tokens ahead and has the big model verify them all in one pass. Right guesses give you two or three tokens for the price of one pass and a bit; wrong guesses cost you the bit. The output does not change either way: the big model only keeps a drafted token it would have produced itself.

Two current models ship with their own drafter. Qwen 3.8 carries a NextN head, one extra layer that predicts the token after the next one. Gemma 4 ships a four-layer assistant model next to the 26B main model. Both now run in dasLLAMA on Metal, on any Apple GPU the engine runs on; the drafter is a second file you load next to the model. We measured on Boris's new M5 Max laptop and on Anton's M4 Pro Mac mini, which he lent us for the week and which answers over ssh from the other side of the globe.

What we tried

How deep to draft, first of all. One draft token means the big model verifies two tokens per pass; two means three, and the second draft only pays if it is accepted often enough to cover a third row. We tried one against two on each machine and let the tuner decide, the way it decides everything else on a box, and every machine we own settled on one. Three and four were so far behind on the development build that they never reached the ruler.

We also looked at drafting wide instead of deep: verifying the two or three most likely tokens at one position rather than a chain. We dropped it on paper. With one token ahead there is no room for a runner-up, and together with depth it multiplies the rows the verify has to pay for.

We dropped the automatic depth controller too, the one that would raise the depth while the drafts keep landing, in favour of the per-box setting. It may come back one day as a per-request setting; the math prompt below explains why.

The Gemma assistant reads the main model's hidden state as its input, and there are two places to read it from, before or after the final norm. After won on acceptance, so after ships. We also checked whether quantizing the main model harder hurts the drafter: the Q8_0 Gemma accepted 76.5% of the drafts, the Q4_K_M one 74.6%. Not much, then.

And then the kernels, which turned out to be the real story and get their own section.

How we measured

The board on daslang.io uses llama-bench, and llama-bench cannot measure speculative decoding. So we built a small ruler for ourselves. It renders four chat prompts through the model's own chat template with thinking off, then runs two engines on the identical rendered text: greedy, exactly 128 new tokens each, three repetitions, one dated and stamped record per machine and model.

Ours runs as the release executable, the same program the board uses, on a sidecar minted the same day - the tuner's picks for that machine, fresh. On Anton's M4 the ruler started it like this, for depth 1:

DAS_TUNE_MANIFEST= DASLLAMA_MTP_HEAD="/Users/dasbox/models/mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q8_0.gguf" "modules/dasLLAMA/performance/_rig/dasllama-bench.app/Contents/MacOS/dasllama-bench" -- -m "/Users/dasbox/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf" --mtp-ab --mtp-depth 1 -n 128 -r 3 --ngl 99 --prompts "modules/dasLLAMA/benchmarks/data/specbench4_prompts.txt" --chat-prompts

llama.cpp runs as its own llama-server, built straight from upstream at commit 6fdd0ac89, exactly as they ship it. The ruler posts the same rendered prompt to its /completion endpoint with ignore_eos set, so it also produces exactly 128 tokens, and reads the server's own timings back. For the same arm on the same machine it started the server as:

"/Users/dasbox/llama.cpp-ref-6fdd0ac/build-stock/bin/llama-server" --port 18790 --host 127.0.0.1 -ngl 99 -fa on -c 2048 -t 10 -np 1 --no-warmup -fit off -m "/Users/dasbox/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf" --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 1 -md "/Users/dasbox/models/mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q8_0.gguf" -ngld 99

The four prompts are the first turns of four tasks from Spec-Bench (hemingkx/Spec-Bench, Apache-2.0): a travel blog post to write, a news article to summarize, a GSM8K arithmetic problem, and a trivia question. Both engines read the same drafter file, and the records carry its checksum.

Two of the ruler's rules exist because each one cost us an afternoon. Same thinking mode on both sides: our very first llama.cpp run had thinking on while ours had it off, and its acceptance read 91%. A thinking-on answer is an outline, not a blog post, a different text with a different acceptance rate; the ruler now renders one prompt and hands the same bytes to both engines. And let the box cool down: a Mac that has been working hard for ten minutes decodes 13 to 18% slower than a cool one, so every arm now waits three minutes on the 27B before it measures. The release executable also runs before anything else. When the measuring program had already run the engine in-process, everything it measured afterwards came out 20% low, for reasons we still find funny.

The whole thing, on Anton's M4, is one line, and everything below reproduces from it on the dates and builds shown:

bin/daslang -jit modules/dasLLAMA/harness/mtp_ruler.das -- -m $HOME/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf --server $HOME/llama.cpp-ref-6fdd0ac/build-stock/bin/llama-server --depths 1,2 -t 10 --settle 180 -o modules/dasLLAMA/performance/records/mtp_m4_Qwen3.8-27B.json

What we measured

So we ran it, and the drafter earns its keep: about one token in five, and not a token more. In parentheses, the acceptance rate. "off" is plain decoding; "depth 1" and "n_max 1" are one draft token in our engine and in llama.cpp; "depth 2" and "n_max 2" are two.

model, machine (date, build) dasLLAMA off depth 1 depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
gemma-4-26B-A4B, Boris's M5 Max (09-02, ecf965ce5) 122.7 145.9 (75.2%) 148.1 (62.6%) 97.7 133.7 142.0
gemma-4-26B-A4B, Anton's M4 Pro (09-02, e58e5a3ba) 59.2 67.5 (74.6%) 55.6 (62.9%) 52.8 67.2 62.5
Qwen3.8-27B, Boris's M5 Max (09-02, 59cad510c) 27.6 33.0 (77.4%) 31.4 (75.1%) 25.2 34.1 33.5
Qwen3.8-27B, Anton's M4 Pro (09-03, 24d13f1d2) 12.7 14.0 (77.4%) 12.4 (75.1%) 11.5 13.8 12.5

Tokens per second over 128 tokens, four prompts, three repetitions; llama.cpp's pooled figure is the mean of its four prompts.

The same drafter drafts the same on both sides, 75 to 94% accepted at the first position depending on the prompt, in both engines. Whatever separates the two columns, it is not the drafting. And the four prompts do not agree with each other at all. Gemma on the M5 Max:

prompt dasLLAMA off depth 1 depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
writing 124.2 144.0 (69.3%) 138.3 (50.8%) 98.2 139.6 (81.4%) 130.8 (60.0%)
summarization 118.1 133.4 (69.3%) 124.6 (54.9%) 95.8 119.8 (70.3%) 126.0 (56.8%)
math 123.9 160.1 (89.6%) 187.9 (88.0%) 98.4 145.8 (89.6%) 163.4 (84.0%)
qa 124.8 148.6 (74.0%) 155.5 (63.4%) 98.2 129.5 (76.4%) 147.9 (70.5%)

Qwen 3.8 on Anton's M4 Pro, the machine that started the second day:

prompt dasLLAMA off depth 1 depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
writing 12.8 13.5 (70.7%) 10.9 (59.3%) 11.5 13.6 (75.0%) 12.3 (66.7%)
summarization 12.6 14.0 (80.3%) 12.0 (71.7%) 11.5 13.8 (81.4%) 12.4 (69.8%)
math 12.8 15.4 (93.9%) 13.6 (86.2%) 11.5 14.5 (93.8%) 13.9 (87.0%)
qa 12.8 13.2 (67.1%) 13.8 (88.0%) 11.5 13.5 (80.0%) 11.5 (62.5%)

The arithmetic of a round

Here is the part we most wanted to write down. A round with one draft token produces, on average, 1 + a tokens, where a is the acceptance rate. So its speedup over plain decoding is (1 + a) / c, with c the cost of the round in plain passes. Turn it around and the tables tell you what a round costs: c = (1 + a) / speedup.

model, machine our round, in passes llama.cpp's round, in passes
gemma, M5 Max 1.75 / 1.19 = 1.47 1.79 / 1.37 = 1.31
gemma, M4 Pro 1.75 / 1.14 = 1.53 1.83 / 1.27 = 1.44
Qwen 3.8, M5 Max 1.77 / 1.20 = 1.48 1.83 / 1.35 = 1.35
Qwen 3.8, M4 Pro 1.77 / 1.10 = 1.61 1.82 / 1.20 = 1.52

Verifying two tokens at once costs both engines about one and a half plain passes. That, not the drafter, caps the gain at 1.1 to 1.2x on a dense 27B: the second row is the same weights read for two inputs instead of one, plus the draft, plus bookkeeping. On Anton's M4 the round's own clocks, against a 78.7 ms plain pass, read draft 7.4 ms, verify 119.0 ms, accept and commit 1.0 ms, replay 0.7 ms. Ninety-three percent of the round is the verify.

It is also why depth 2 falls behind on the M4 and only breaks even on the M5. A third row costs another half to a whole pass, and the second draft is accepted 51 to 66% of the time, which does not cover it. The math prompt is the exception: there the second draft lands 86 to 88%, and depth 2 comes out ahead on every machine, 187.9 against 160.1 for Gemma on the M5. Acceptance is a property of the text, not the box, which is why the per-request setting may come back one day.

Where the two days went

Back to that morning. Anton's machine read 12.7 tokens per second plain and 11.0 with the drafter on. llama.cpp on the same machine read 11.5 and 13.6. Without that second pair, a verify that cost two full passes for two rows would have looked like the price of a smaller GPU. With it, it looked like what it was. As Boris put it, it is a lot easier when you have an oracle; otherwise how do you know you are slow?

The kernel lab said the same in numbers. Our two-row verify kernel - one pass over the weights serving two input rows - cost 1.36 to 1.49 times two single-row passes on the M4 Pro, and 0.52 to 0.89 on the M5 Max. Same code, two verdicts: the two chips have very different amounts of arithmetic per byte of memory bandwidth, and this kernel is bound by arithmetic. A kernel written in the shape llama.cpp uses sat at 0.9 to 1.05 on the M4. So we wrote a new form for M4-class chips, a register tile where each GPU thread holds two weight rows and feeds both from one read of the input. The tuner tries both forms on a box and keeps the faster. The M4 took the new one, 0.48 ms against the old form's 0.84 on the test shape; the M5 kept the old one, 0.49 against 0.53. The M4 row went to 13.9.

Then Boris asked why the depth-2 row was dropping like crazy: 7.9 tokens per second, 0.62 of plain. Same story, one row up. Three rows took a four-column kernel nobody had ever tried on this chip, and on the M4 it costs 1.3 to 1.5 times four single passes. We already had all the pieces - "and 1 + 2 is better than 3", as Boris said - so three rows now run as the new two-row form plus one single pass, wherever the tuner picked that form. Depth 2 went from 7.9 to 12.4 and depth 1 to 14.0 by the evening of the 3rd. About a hundred lines and a test. Finding it took a yardstick.

The yardstick

Glad we have llama.cpp next to every number here. It is the gold standard of running language models on your own machine, the only way we know whether we are fast, and the only way we know when to stop: the second day ended where it did because the two columns had met. Both projects are open source. Anything in this engine is theirs for the taking, with the license's attribution, and the same goes the other way. On these prompts, on these two machines, on these two days: plain decoding is 10 to 26% faster in dasLLAMA, the speculative rounds land within a few percent of each other in both directions, and llama.cpp's depth-2 round is cheaper than ours. That one is ours to fix, and it is what winter evenings are for.

entry.title: Apple M5 support lands - text, vision and speech, tuned on the new silicon.
entry.content: dasLLAMA now treats the Apple M5 as a first-class target: the Metal 4 tensor units where the per-box race crowns them, the vision and speech encoders on the GPU, and the CPU lane on the M5 Max's all-compute core layout. The full M5 Max board is re-minted and on the board - gemma-4-E2B Q8_0 at 9074.3 / 161.3 tok/s (llama.cpp 7413.4 / 137.0), Qwen3.8-27B at 913.9 / 27.8 (752.1 / 25.4), pp512 / tg128 on Metal. Bringing a chip up one model at a time, and why it was fun: the story.

entry.title: Boris got a new laptop.
entry.content:
Boris got a new laptop. An M5 Max, at the end of August, and it became the main machine the same afternoon. dasLLAMA had never run on an M5. Anton lent us his Mac mini - an M4 Pro, the previous generation, sitting on the other side of the globe and reached over ssh - so we could watch the two chips side by side. And we got to work.

What a new chip is, to this engine

dasLLAMA does not ship kernels tuned for a chip. For every heavy operation - a matrix multiply, an attention step, a normalization - it ships several ways of computing the same thing. The first time it runs on a machine it tries them all, keeps the fastest of each, and writes the picks into a small file called a sidecar. Sixty-two such choices for the M5 Max. So "supporting the M5" was not a port. It was letting the tuner run and then looking hard at every place where the pick had changed.

Three places did.

The M5's GPU has tensor units - dedicated matrix hardware, reached through Apple's Metal 4 tensor API. For each matrix multiply in the engine we wrote a tensor-unit version next to the plain one and let the machine choose. On the M5 Max the tensor version came out ahead in 23 of them: every multiply over the compressed 4-, 5-, 6- and 8-bit weights, the 16-bit ones, the expert layers of the mixture-of-experts models, and the attention scores. The choice lives in the sidecar, not in the code: a machine that never tried keeps the plain version, and one that tried and found it slower keeps it too.

On the CPU side, the M5 Max has no Efficiency cores at all. It has 6 cores Apple calls Super and 12 it calls Performance, and all of them are the real thing. On Anton's M4 we had taught the CPU lane to leave the Efficiency cores out of the worker pool, because they only slowed everyone down. On the M5 that habit would have quietly thrown away a third of the chip. Now all 18 work, and token generation parks the six slower ones. We could not believe our eyes, so we checked it twice, on both machines.

The vision towers and the speech-to-text encoders run on the GPU on the M5 the way the text path does. Nothing new in the design - the same GPU plumbing - but each one had to be tried again and its picks re-made.

What we measured

So we measured it on the M5 and - look at that. What a beast of a machine.

model dasLLAMA (pp512 / tg128) llama.cpp (pp512 / tg128)
gemma-4-E2B Q8_0 9074.3 / 161.3 7413.4 / 137.0
Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M 913.9 / 27.8 752.1 / 25.4
Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M 3752.9 / 165.7 3422.4 / 137.0
gpt-oss-20b mxfp4 3995.1 / 162.7 3476.6 / 149.0

Before and after, one chip generation apart, on the same 27B model: Anton's M4 Pro reads 126.4 / 12.9, the new laptop 913.9 / 27.8. Prompt processing moved seven times. Token generation, which is bound by memory bandwidth, a little over twice. llama.cpp shows the same picture, 126.3 / 11.5 on the M4 and 752.1 / 25.4 on the M5.

The models that do more than text ride the same machine, the same day. gemma-4-12B's vision tower takes 7.1 ms where llama.cpp's multimodal path takes 95 ms; Qwen2.5-Omni's window vision transformer 106 ms against 118 ms.

Speech, too. whisper large-v3-turbo transcribes the short JFK clip that whisper.cpp ships as its sample in 140 ms, against whisper-cli's 153 ms on the same GPU. Canary-Qwen, NVIDIA's speech-to-text model, in its new 8-bit form does the same clip in 307.6 ms on the M5 and 512.9 ms on the M4, where NVIDIA's own NeMo on Torch MPS takes 704.7 ms and 1076.5 ms. On the long gb1 clip we read 6484 ms and NeMo 4383 ms, which gives us something to do during the long winter evenings.

Glad we have llama.cpp, whisper.cpp and NeMo numbers next to ours. Those are the industry standard for this kind of thing, and they are the only way we know whether we are fast, and the only way we know when to stop. Without a yardstick a new chip is just a machine that runs, and every one of these numbers would be a little worse.

Sixty-two kernels walked into a new chip.

Most walked out the same. Twenty-three swapped to the tensor units. A few found out, in the first afternoon, that the form that had carried them for two generations was now the slow one, and had to be rewritten before the tuner had anything worth picking. None of this is visible from a spec sheet. It all happily went into the tuner log, and so did our last week - which probably says something about us.

entry.title: Qwen 3.8 27B joins the board - the new dense hybrid runs on CPU and Metal.
entry.content:
Qwen 3.8 27B is out, and it needed no new architecture support in dasLLAMA: the 3.8 generation keeps the qwen3.5 architecture - Gated-DeltaNet recurrent layers interleaved 3:1 with gated full attention - so it loads on the existing family path as a pure scale-up. The Q4_K_M file's attention and FFN planes serve natively on the kq rails, CPU and Metal alike (the DeltaNet projections transcode to q8 at load), and the model joins the official board catalog.

On an M1 Max (pp512 / tg128, llama-bench protocol): Metal - das 147.0 / 14.5 tok/s, llama.cpp 137.6 / 11.5; CPU - das 33.2 / 5.8, llama.cpp 29.8 / 5.6. On an M4 Pro: Metal - das 127.0 / 12.8, llama.cpp 126.2 / 11.5; CPU - das 45.8 / 11.6, llama.cpp 40.4 / 11.0. Full rows for both boxes are on the board.

entry.title: Metal support lands in speech-to-text - whisper large-v3-turbo at 49x realtime on an M1 Max.
entry.content: Speech-to-text now serves on Metal: whisper's cross-attention and decoder run on the GPU by default on Apple silicon, and the full-GPU mode powers the new gpu category on the board. On an M1 Max, whisper large-v3-turbo transcribes a 3:19 clip in 4.0 s - 49x realtime, against 36x for whisper.cpp's Metal path and 12x for our CPU lane. The board now splits ASR into the same cpu / cpu + accel / gpu categories the LLM board has.

entry.title: dasllama.io is live - news, the full ladder, and the sidecar exchange.
entry.content: Everything measured now lives here, community submissions included. daslang.io/dasllama.html stays the promotional scoreboard and carries official measurements only.
